content.p: When North Korea's army crossed the border on 25 June 1950, South Korea's government was already holding tens of thousands of political prisoners and had enrolled hundreds of thousands more people in an official scheme meant to reform suspected leftists. Soon afterwards, as its own army fell back, the southern authorities began shooting prisoners and rounding up the members of that scheme, the National Guidance Alliance, known in English as the Bodo League. The Associated Press has described a "secretive slaughter" believed to have killed 100,000 or more leftists and supposed sympathisers in a few weeks of mid-1950, usually without charge or trial.

Nobody has fixed the number. South Korea's Truth and Reconciliation Commission called 100,000 a conservative estimate, a legal journal summarising its work says its final report found that the government took part in the killing of over 200,000 civilians, and after 2005 the commission began opening burial pits that families had long kept silent about. The sections below follow how the killings were organised, what is known about particular sites, who watched, and why so much remains unsettled.

The groundwork was political. In 1947, two years after Washington and Moscow divided Korea, the US military government declared the Korean Labor Party, the southern communists, illegal. Once Syngman Rhee's government gained sovereignty in 1948 it suppressed all leftist activity and put down a guerrilla uprising. The Sydney Morning Herald, writing about the commission's findings, noted that the new government had also ordered its army to crush a leftist revolt on Cheju Island in 1948, where about 30,000 local people were gunned down. By the time the northern invasion came, the AP reported, Rhee's regime held up to 30,000 political prisoners.

The National Guidance Alliance was the second instrument. The AP described it as a "re-education" body with 300,000 members, to which the authorities had assigned leftist sympathisers and which also took in illiterate peasants who had been drawn in with promises of jobs and other benefits. The Hankyoreh newspaper gave the same description, adding that the leftists were assigned on the pretext of protecting them from execution. Membership was not a reliable sign of anything. In one case the Hankyoreh recounted, a Gimhae man who had been jailed for taking part in the March 1 independence movement was not a member of the alliance, according to his grandson. It is presumed, the paper wrote, that right-wing youths singled him out, dragged him off and executed him on Nabat Ridge after the war began.

When the war began on 25 June 1950, the Hankyoreh wrote, preliminary detentions started for alliance members across the country. The AP reported that on 29 June, as the southern army and its American advisers retreated, reports from Seoul said that the northerners had emptied the capital's prisons and that former inmates were reinforcing the new occupation regime. Fear that prisoners and alliance members would cooperate with the advancing army is what the commission later said lay behind many of the killings.

In the port city of Busan, an American adviser, Lieutenant Colonel Rollins Emmerich, wrote in a confidential account for Army historians that a South Korean regimental commander, Colonel Kim Chong-won, planned "to execute some 3500 suspected peace time Communists, locked up in the local prison". Emmerich told him that the enemy was not as close as Kim feared and that "atrocities could not be condoned". But he also, the AP wrote, indicated conditional acceptance: Kim was told that if the enemy reached the outskirts he "would be permitted to open the gates of the prison and shoot the prisoners with machine guns". The AP called the passage, which was left out of the published Army history, the first documentation found showing advance sanction by the US military for such killings. Emmerich also wrote that he persuaded officials in Daegu, 55 miles north of Busan, "at that time" not to execute 4,500 prisoners at once; within weeks, according to the AP, hundreds were being executed in the Daegu area.

As the summer wore on, Korean and foreign witnesses later said, Busan-area prisoners were shot by the hundreds, the AP reported. The Sydney Morning Herald, writing in 2008, said the picture emerging was that about 10,000 prisoners were eventually trucked out of Busan and machine-gunned. That is well above the 1,500 for the Busan area that the commission confirmed, and the two figures sit side by side in the record.
content.h2: What the commission confirmed in the south and east
content.p: The Hankyoreh reported that the commission announced that at least 3,400 civilians and inmates held at prisons in Busan, Masan and Jinju had been illegally killed by soldiers and police between July and September 1950. It said this was the first time a state institution had formally confirmed that retreating military and police personnel killed prison inmates indiscriminately. According to the commission's findings, at least 1,500 inmates and alliance members were killed by prison guards and regional police, among them members of the Counterintelligence Corps in the Busan region, in three attacks between 26 July and 25 September. They had been taken out on the pretext of transfer to another prison, and were shot at places such as Dongmae-san and the Jang-san ravine or drowned in the sea off Oryuk Island. At least 717 inmates and alliance members from Masan Prison were shot or thrown into the sea, and at least 1,200 victims were killed at Jinju Prison, 576 of them identified.

A commission representative drew a legal conclusion from this. "It may have been wartime, but it was a criminal act to illegally execute prison inmates and civilian members of the National Guidance Alliance," the representative said, because the victims were killed in areas under South Korean control, only out of fear that they might help the advancing North Korean army. Most of the inmates, the representative said, were not death-penalty cases but prisoners with sentences of under three years, some for breaches of the army's criminal code. Where a court-martial had sentenced a prisoner to death, the commission said the proceeding was a formality and in effect no different from a mass execution.

A second Hankyoreh report on the commission's work concerned the Yeongcheon area in North Gyeongsang. The commission confirmed that at least 239 former leftists in the alliance and villagers near the Nakdong River front were killed by local police and the troops stationed there between July and September 1950. Counting victims whose identities were not confirmed, an official put the estimate at around 600. The commission said alliance members there were killed over a long period, out of fear that they might side with North Korea, because the area was a place of strategic importance where the armies fought hand to hand. It identified smaller atrocities too, such as the killing of a deserter's family and 14 villagers with the same surname, and another 50 villagers in Gujeon-ri and Donam-dong because a landowner was supposedly a leftist activist. The commission said the killings were led by army and police intelligence on orders from the Counter Intelligence Corps, a special operations unit, and that American counter-intelligence knew about them.

The best-documented killing field was outside Daejeon, in central South Korea. In July 1950, the AP reported, American officers photographed the shooting of dozens of men at the site. Kim Dong-choon, the commissioner overseeing the investigation, told the AP that the dead there are believed to number between 3,000 and 7,000, shot by their own country's military and police and put into mass graves. The Sydney Morning Herald, citing the commission, said prisoners were shuttled from the city jail to the edge of long trenches, made to lie down and shot, with up to 7,000 executed over days. A US Army major took photographs that reached Washington within a month and were then suppressed for half a century.

The AP's archive search found further episodes. An Air Force intelligence officer, Donald Nichols, wrote in a 1981 memoir that he witnessed and photographed the shooting of an estimated 1,800 prisoners at Suwon, 20 miles south of Seoul, in the first days of July. In mid-August the American commander Douglas MacArthur, in Tokyo, learned of a mass shooting near Daegu in which 200 to 300 people died, including women and a girl of 12 or 13, from a top-secret Army report describing the "extreme cruelty" of the South Korean military police. Bodies fell into a ravine, and hours later, a US military policeman wrote, some "were still alive and moaning". MacArthur took no action beyond referring the report to the ambassador, John J. Muccio, who later wrote that he had urged South Korean officials to carry out executions humanely and with due process. On 15 August, Brig. Gen. Francis W. Farrell, the chief US military adviser to the South Koreans, recommended that the command investigate; the AP found no sign that anyone did. A month later the Daejeon photographs were sent to the Pentagon with a colonel's report that the South Koreans had killed "thousands" of political prisoners. In December, W.J. Sebald, the State Department's liaison to MacArthur, cabled that the command viewed the killings as a South Korean "internal matter" and had "refrained from taking any action".

The British intervened in places. On 7 December in occupied North Korea, according to news reports the AP cited, British officers stopped the shooting of 21 civilians who had been lined up, by threatening to shoot the South Korean officer responsible, and later that month British troops seized "Execution Hill" outside Seoul to prevent further mass killings. The South Koreans barred journalists from execution sites, the AP wrote, and the US Army eventually blamed all the Daejeon deaths on the North Koreans, who had carried out their own executions of rightists there and elsewhere.

Historians split over what this means. Bruce Cumings of the University of Chicago sees a share of American guilt: after the fact, he said, the US "not only did nothing, but covered up the Daejeon massacres". Allan R. Millett, an emeritus professor at Ohio State, said, "I'm not sure there's enough evidence to pin culpability on these guys". Jung Byung-joon, a historian on the commission, said of the Americans: "The most important thing is that they did not stop the executions." He added: "They were at the crime scene, and took pictures and wrote reports." Koh Chung-ryol, whose father's bones lie in the Sannae valley near Daejeon, said bereaved families believed the United States bore some responsibility, though they could not present concrete evidence. Frank Winslow, a military adviser at Daejeon, said that the Koreans were sovereign and responsible for their own actions.

The swiftness and nationwide scale of the roundups point to orders from the top, from President Rhee and his security chiefs, Korean historians told the AP. Those officials are dead and Korean documentary evidence is scarce. In its Yeongcheon findings the commission, for its part, said responsibility lay not only with the army and police but with their superiors at the Martial Law Command, and ultimately with the state that was supposed to manage them.

Few of those who took part have spoken. One who did was Kim Man-sik, 82 when the BBC interviewed him. A former soldier, he said his unit was ordered on two occasions to collect suspected leftists from the police: "we conducted group executions". He asked for an understanding of the circumstances, saying that his forces were "very disadvantaged" and "cornered", and that his military policemen felt they had little choice but to follow orders. The legal journal's account of the commission's final report notes that the commission did not identify specific people responsible for the massacres, and links that restraint to a reluctance in Korean society to name perpetrators.

For much of the postwar period, the BBC reported, South Korea's military dictatorships made an investigation impossible. Families suffered in silence: after the war, said Lee Tae-joon, whose cousin disappeared at the start of the war, even a hint that a family had leftist sympathies left it open to hostility and hatred. There was a brief opening after the revolution of 19 April 1960. In Gimhae and Changwon a funeral committee dug up 272 bodies, and only one, a man with a gold-capped tooth, was identified. After the military coup of 16 May 1961, the Hankyoreh recounted, the committee's director, Kim Yeong-uk, was charged under a new special law and sentenced to seven years in prison in January 1962. The verdict from the revolutionary court said surviving-family activity would make ordinary people doubt the national policy of anti-communism. Asked what crime it was to bury his father's remains, he was told by the prosecutor, according to his son, "It is a crime to bury Reds." His son recalled that after his release the man was repeatedly taken away and brought back half-dead whenever a spy case arose.

The legislature approved the legislation that established the commission, a framework act on clearing up past incidents. The sources disagree on the date: the legal journal says the National Assembly passed it in May 2005, the Hankyoreh says it was passed on 1 December 2005, and the Sydney Morning Herald says the commission was set up that December. It had 15 commissioners, about 240 staff, a budget of about 19.7 billion won, and a remit covering abuses between 1910 and 1987, according to the journal and the BBC. The BBC reported that its staff had interviewed hundreds of witnesses and relatives and had begun digging the year before its report. It lacked the power to compel witnesses or to impose sanctions, and its supporters feared its mandate was too short, the BBC added.

When the BBC visited, only a handful of 160 suspected mass-grave sites had been uncovered. One was an abandoned cobalt mine near Daegu where a team of archaeologists was uncovering bones; it is thought to hold the bodies of up to 3,000 people executed and thrown into a vertical shaft. The AP said the commission recovered the remains of more than 400 people at four sites in 2007, and that it believed the purge had filled some 150 mass graves by the autumn of 1950. Its president, the historian Ahn Byung-ook, said the commission planned to ask the US government for an overall investigation once it finished the cases involving the US Army.

The commission's work was cut short. The legal journal says the commission's efforts to find remains were cut short by a change of leadership in 2008, when President Lee Myung-bak came to power. The journal says Lee regarded such commissions as standing in the way of his economic aims, and he appointed new leaders to the body, and that the commission closed without completing its mandate. Its final report, the journal says, made 17 recommendations, among them proper burial for the victims, local memorial services and an effort to obtain evidence from the United States. The Hankyoreh noted that the commission had at one point completed its investigations of 1,638 out of 2,413 alliance-related incidents, leaving 775 still open.

The commission's recommendations went beyond digging. For the Busan, Masan and Jinju prison killings and the Yeongcheon case it advised the state to apologise, support memorial projects, help bereaved families and teach peace and human rights to army and police personnel, according to the Hankyoreh.

For families, the largest question is still the apology. Kim Gwang-ho, whose grandfather was seized and whose father went to prison for burying the dead, told the Hankyoreh that he wanted to hear "a true apology for the things the state did to my grandfather and father". He asked what meaning the 60th anniversary of the Korean War could have if it passed with fireworks and no true reconciliation.
